newsitem.title: INDIA: Enron India unit seen luring foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: Enron India unit seen luring foreign funds.

text.p: U.S. energy giant Enron Corp's controversial Indian power plant will help attract foreign investment to the tune of $2.5 billion when complete, company officials said on Thursday.

Enron Corp Chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay told a news conference that the 2,450 MW power plant would draw foreign investors into India's western Maharashtra state, where the plant is located, once cheap power became available.
"When the first phase is completed, it will attract about one billion dollars in foreign investment," Lay said. "The second phase is expected to atttract another $1.5 billion."
The plant would help boost the industrial development of the area, Lay added.

The 740-MW first phase of the Dabhol Power Company (DPC)'s $2.3 billion plant will go on line by December 1998, Lay said. The 1440-MW second phase is expected to be completed by 2001, company officials said.

Work on the plant was delayed for over a year because of a political tug-of-war between the Congress state government which negotiated the contract, and the Hindu nationalist coalition which defeated it in local polls in March 1995.
The Hindu nationalists scrapped the project in August 1995 because they said it was too expensive. Work resumed last December after the terms of the deal were renegotiated.
The project is a multifuel facility capable of using either naphtha or distillate in the first phase, but it is envisaged to be gas-fired once the second phase is commissioned.

"We will use naphtha for the first phase," said Rebecca Mark, CEO of the Enron Development Corp, the Enron arm that is supervising the Dabhol operations. "But it is our intention to get the gas in as fast as possible."
The liquefied natural gas (LNG) to be used by the plant will be obtained from Enron's Qatar unit, Dabhol president Sanjay Bhatnagar said.
Enron's DPC was one of eight fast track projects designed to lure foreign private investment into India's crumbling infrastructure sector shortly after open market reforms were launched in 1991.
